articles.title: Sales of trainers dive at JD Sports as cost of living pressures bite
articles.summary: Inflation deterring shoppers from spending, especially in the US, says high street chain. The sports fashion retailer JD has cut its profit forecasts as cost of living pressures, fuelled by the US war on Iran, weighed on sales of trainers.
body: JD Sports, which sells brands including Nike and Adidas, said widespread inflation had hit shoppers’ wallets, resulting in a drop in sales across important markets such as the US, where it struggled to shift trainers and other footwear.

Bosses went on to warn that the wider fall in consumer spending was likely to continue into the second half of the year, leading to lower-than-expected profits. The retailer now expects pre-tax profits of between £700m and £800m for the full year, having previously hoped to reach £750m to £850m.
The news led to a 12% drop in JD’s London-listed shares on Thursday morning to their lowest level since July.

Régis Schultz, chief executive, said: “Trading in the second quarter remained tough,” t adding that the company had been forced to cut prices and offer promotional sales to compensate, as “our core consumer was impacted by incremental cost of living pressures.”

articles.title: ‘The only way is up’: cycling Norway’s mountainous ‘Milky Way’
articles.summary: The Mjølkevegen was once used to bring milk from high pastures to the towns below. Now cyclists are discovering the road’s breathtaking panoramas of peaks and lakes, dotted with cosy inns. ‘Norway is a hilly country,” shrugs Glenn Roar Berge. He’s not wrong, though he is fond of an understatement.
body: For most of our three-day ride, we’ll be following the Mjølkevegen, or Milky Way, a 155-mile (250km) route from Vinstra in the north to Gol in the south. It was developed after the second world war, when increased demand for fresh milk meant connecting the mountain farms with the towns below. While farming continues, the road has been embraced in recent years by gravel cyclists, (typically riders on drop-bar bikes favouring unpaved roads and trails), looking for a multi-day adventure far from towns and cities.

Ruten Fjellstue is a traditional inn, set up for cross-country skiing in winter, hiking and biking in summer. My trip starts here and it’s where I’ll meet my guide and group, and pick up my hired bike. It’s set high above the valley and painted falun red – the iron-oxide agricultural paint typical across Nordic countries. Berit and Arthur are the third-generation owners. I arrive late, so Arthur picks me up from Vinstra train station (about three hours north-west of Oslo) and Berit has kept a home-cooked meal warm: a generous plate of fish with potatoes, vegetables and cream sauce, followed by apple crumble.

articles.summary: Five hundred people turn up to adopt plants from conservatory that will reopen in 2030 after renovation project. body: This precarious situation has caused the estate to shutter its greenhouse on the third and fourth floors for three years so a full refurbishment can take place. But the hiatus has a silver lining for many of those who visited on Wednesday to give the plants from the conservatory a new home.
Five hundred people turned up to pick up a cutting from the Barbican’s plant collection and were asked to fill out an “adoption form” as if they were taking home a pet.
Lydia Goldberg, 56, a tech worker, was one of the first through the door and selected a pretty, silvery-green Swedish ivy plant.

“I am a houseplant lover,” she said. “I live in the Barbican and my bedroom overlooks the conservatory. I am sad to see it close but it’s great that it’s being restored. Having a piece of the conservatory in my flat will be incredible and this is a real community event. I can see quite a few of my neighbours here!”

articles.title: It used to be our imperfect bodies that made us insecure. With AI, it’s our minds as well
articles.summary: For most of modern history, technology sought to imitate humans. Humans increasingly seek to imitate technology. Two faces that appeared on my Instagram feed in recent months gave me pause. One belonged to John Travolta at Cannes.
body: In any case the feeling lasted only a second: a flicker of unease, as though I were looking at people who had become approximations of themselves.

There is a name for that sensation. In a 1970 article, the Japanese robotics professor Masahiro Mori described what he called the “uncanny valley”. He found that robots that were designed to look as human as possible often provoked discomfort in people. That was a surprise, since the benefit of humanoid robots was supposed to be that we humans would trust them more.

What scares us about a robot that almost passes as human? One explanation may be that we sense danger when encountering something we cannot categorise easily as either human or not. Another is that the features that seem “off”, such as glossy skin or frozen expressions, resemble signs of disease or death.

articles.title: The 9 Major Benefits of Walking After Dinner
articles.summary: Walking after eating is proven to benefit our overall health. Here, Heather Viola, DO, primary-care physician at Mount Sinai Doctors-Ansonia breaks down all the reasons why and how to incorporate it into your daily routine.
body: After a big meal at night, even the lightest form of physical activity may be the furthest thing from your mind. But as it turns out, walking after eating has many benefits.

We’re not just talking about boosting our endorphins or reducing stress levels when taking a leisurely, serotonin-inducing strolls. Walking after eating has been proven to do many things for our overall health, and it’s definitely something to consider for future meals. But don’t just take our word for it. Below, Heather Viola, DO, primary-care physician at Mount Sinai Doctors-Ansonia, breaks down all the reasons you should be taking a post-meal walk after breakfast, lunch, or dinner.

Both times can be beneficial, just in different ways. Dr. Viola explains that walking before your body has ingested food will enact different chemical reactions than walking after eating. Walking before a meal helps burn stored fat efficiently and assists with weight loss. When you walk half an hour or so after eating, she says, it can decrease the amount of sugar and fats that accumulate in your bloodstream. It can also give your body more energy to exercise, digest, and regulate blood sugar levels more effectively.
points: Walking after eating is proven to benefit our overall health.

articles.title: On the Podcast: How Mark Guiducci Is Putting His Stamp on Vanity Fair
articles.summary: For this Thursday’s episode of “The Run Through,“ Chloe Malle spoke with her longtime friend (and former Vogue colleague) Mark Guiducci, the global editorial director of Vanity Fair, just days before the launch of his September cover, featuring Marc Jacobs.
body: “I think in some ways [Marc] is the greatest American fashion designer,” Guiducci said. “And if Marc Jacobs has nine lives, he’s maybe on his seventh.”

The cover story, written by José Criales-Unzueta, chronicles a transitional moment for Jacobs, whose namesake brand was sold by LVMH to WHP Global and G-III Apparel Group this year. “This new chapter of Marc’s professional life is something different than going public and having umpteen thousands of stores around the world...and yet Marc is his own version of success,” Guiducci said.

But of course, it wouldn’t be a reunion without some reminiscing about the old days of Vogue. Sitting in a podcast studio no larger than the office they shared nearly 15 years ago, the two laughed over wellness routines and after-hours dinner plans.

Also on the podcast, Vogue ’s senior lifestyle and weddings editor Liam Hess chatted about how the week’s biggest wedding stories ( Jordyn Woods! Tallulah Willis! Cris y Gio!) came to be. Plus, we close out our Dogue days of summer with the final covers!

articles.title: ‘Novak Djokovic: The Wolf in Winter’ Is the Best Tennis Film in Years
articles.summary: Directed by Jason Hehir—best-known for the Michael Jordan documentary “The Last Dance”—“The Wolf in Winter” gives us the most complete portrayal of the 24-time Grand Slam winner that we've yet seen.
body: There’s been a bumper crop of sports documentaries recently—everything from reality series à la Drive to Survive and its various imitators to those focused on a single standout athlete—say, Beckham or Pelé. And tennis, for so long something of an also-ran in terms of off-court cultural cachet, has, if anything, now more than its fair share of well-done docs—from the moving Chris & Martina: The Final Set to Naomi Osaka, Carlos Alcaraz: My Way, Federer: Twelve Final Days, and the recent, gripping, four-part Rafa, centered on Rafael Nadal’s almost lifelong struggle to overcome an assortment of injuries as he took his place among the game’s all-time greats.

The newest member of this club: Novak Djokovic: The Wolf in Winter, which premieres today on Prime Video. Directed by Jason Hehir—best known for the acclaimed The Last Dance miniseries, which explored Michael Jordan’s final season with the Chicago Bulls— The Wolf in Winter is notable, in many ways, for what it isn’t. This isn’t a collection of highlight reels, nor is it a paint-by-numbers biography that tells the predictable inspirational story of early talent and overcoming fierce battles, with lessons learned along the way.
points: Directed by Jason Hehir—best-known for the Michael Jordan documentary “The Last Dance”—“The Wolf in Winter” gives us the most complete portrayal of the 24-time Grand Slam winner that we've yet seen.

articles.title: Why Anthony Bourdain’s Editor Wanted ‘Tony’ to Be Darker
articles.summary: There are two types of biopics: those that unconventionally show, and those that exhaustively tell. Thank goodness that Tony, the highly anticipated A24 biopic about the late Anthony Bourdain, takes the former route.
body: Eater spoke with the film’s screenwriters about casting the titular role, chef cameos, and more BTS moments.

Then again, successfully pitching a Bourdain biopic to his estate was always going to be a big swing. I spoke with Todd Bartels and Lou Howe about what made that swing possible (for one: bringing on Kimberly Witherspoon, Bourdain’s literary agent and friend, as an executive producer); which cast member demonstrated the best culinary chops; and who they could imagine playing an older, more seasoned Anthony Bourdain.
Eater: How did you strike the balance between making a movie for the passionate Anthony Bourdain fans, and viewers who may know very little about him?

Lou Howe: I was anxious about that [ laughs ], especially at the very beginning. But [we] just [tried] to make a good movie, and hope that the entertainment factor and emotional engagement hits the target well enough. We started this whole process as fans, so in that way we felt relatively comfortable servicing fellow fans. You want to write a good story that people can plug into no matter who the character is. Of course, there are some Kitchen Confidential Easter eggs.
points: There are two types of biopics: those that unconventionally show, and those that exhaustively tell.
Thank goodness that Tony, the highly anticipated A24 biopic about the late Anthony Bourdain, takes the former route.

articles.title: 5 Exciting Hotel Openings on the Mediterranean Coast That Are a Design Lover's Dream
articles.summary: The most exciting hotels opening in Southern Europe put local heritage and artisanship first.
body: Opened in May, this escape is the brainchild of Christopher and Suzanne Sharp, the founders of The Rug Company. She was born on the island, they bought the 18th-century palazzo together in 2010, and he spent the years since filling the gardens with jasmine and bougainvillea. In the way that Malta has long lived at the crossroads of Europe, so too does the characterful 17-room property. Hand-painted pottery from nearby ceramics studio Villa Bologna (owned by Sharp scion Sophie) share rooms with Sicilian marble tables and glass fixtures from Murano.

This May, Zannier added to its smattering of immersive design hotels a 17-acre private island along the Côte d'Azur. Owned by the Ricard family of Pastis fame, it's now a beautiful, laid-back retreat steeped in Provençal tradition. A ferry connects the mainland to this car-free village-as-resort, where existing structures like two-story former fishermen's houses are now villas courtesy of Paris firms Hardel Le Bihan Architectes and Niez Studio Paysagistes. Crafts workshops for guests are held three times a week in a converted warehouse.
